title: Oats vs. Rice: Fiber, Protein, and Satiety

seo.title: Oats vs. Rice: Fiber, Protein, and Satiety
seo.meta_description: Cooked oats usually have much more fiber than white rice and contain beta-glucan. Compare protein, fiber, calories, and fullness on an equal basis.
seo.search_intent: Compare oats and rice for fiber, protein, and how filling they are.

excerpt: Cooked oatmeal generally provides substantially more fiber than cooked white rice, while protein per 100 grams is surprisingly similar. Oat beta-glucan and the viscous texture of porridge may also support greater feelings of fullness.
content_html:
Oats and rice are both grains, but they are usually eaten in very different forms. Oats become a water-rich porridge; rice is commonly served as separate cooked grains. To compare them fairly, keep the preparation state the same. Comparing dry oats with cooked rice makes the oats look artificially nutrient-dense because the water content is completely different.

Fiber is the clearest difference

Cooked oatmeal made with water provides roughly 1.7 grams of fiber per 100 grams. Cooked white rice is closer to 0.4 gram, while cooked brown rice is around 1.6 grams.

So oats have a large fiber advantage over white rice, but the difference becomes much smaller when rice is whole grain.

Protein is closer than many people expect

Per 100 grams cooked, oatmeal provides about 2.5 grams of protein. Cooked white rice is around 2.7 grams and brown rice about 2.7–2.8 grams. Those numbers are close because cooked oatmeal contains a great deal of water.

On a dry-weight basis oats are more protein-rich, but that is not the same comparison as what lands in the bowl.

Why oatmeal often feels more filling

Oats contain beta-glucan, a soluble fiber that can increase viscosity in the digestive tract. A review of human studies found that most evidence supports a positive effect of oat beta-glucan on perceived satiety, although results vary by dose, processing, and food form.

A bowl of porridge also carries a lot of water, creating volume for a moderate amount of energy. Satiety, however, is not determined by one nutrient: toppings, portion size, protein foods, and how quickly the meal is eaten all matter.

Brown rice closes the fiber gap

Brown rice retains the bran and has substantially more fiber than white rice. USDA MyPlate recommends making at least half of grain choices whole grains and lists both oatmeal and brown rice as whole-grain options.

Which one should you choose?

For breakfast or a meal where soluble fiber and a thick, high-volume texture are useful, oats have a clear advantage. Rice is more neutral and versatile as a savory base, and brown rice provides more fiber than white.

Bottom line: oats beat white rice on fiber and have a plausible satiety advantage; cooked protein values are similar, and brown rice narrows the fiber difference considerably.

faq.question: Do oats have more protein than rice?
faq.answer: On a dry basis, usually yes. Per 100 grams cooked, however, oatmeal and rice can have similar protein because they absorb different amounts of water.

faq.question: Which has more fiber, oatmeal or white rice?
faq.answer: Cooked oatmeal is roughly 1.7 g/100 g versus about 0.4 g/100 g for cooked white rice.

faq.question: Is brown rice more filling than white rice?
faq.answer: It can be because it contains more fiber, but the overall meal and serving size have a large effect on fullness.
